questions.question: What's the difference between SAST, DAST, SCA, IAST, and pen testing — and how do you build a practical security testing pipeline for a Java/Spring Boot service?
questions.title: Security Testing for Java: SAST, DAST, SCA, IAST, Pen Testing in CI/CD
questions.direct_answer: Security testing is **a layered set of techniques**, not one tool: **SAST** (static analysis of source/bytecode — SonarQube, Semgrep, CodeQL, Snyk Code, SpotBugs/Find-Sec-Bugs) catches vulnerabilities at code level early; **SCA** (Software Composition Analysis — Snyk, OWASP Dependency-Check, Dependabot, Renovate) finds vulnerable third-party deps; **DAST** (dynamic analysis of running apps — OWASP ZAP, Burp Suite) tests the deployed service for runtime issues like injection, broken auth; **IAST** (instrumented app, hybrid — Contrast, Seeker) catches issues during functional tests with low false positives; **container/IaC scanning** (Trivy, Grype, Checkov, tfsec) for images and infrastructure; **secret scanning** (gitleaks, trufflehog) prevents key leaks; **pen testing** (manual + creative) finds business-logic and chained vulnerabilities tools miss. A practical pipeline: pre-commit (secret scan + lint) → PR checks (SAST + SCA + unit security tests) → build (container scan + IaC scan) → staging (DAST + IAST during integration tests) → production (runtime monitoring, periodic pen tests, bug bounty). Don't try to deploy all tools at once — start with **SCA + secret scanning + SAST**, then add DAST + container scanning. Tune aggressively: false-positive fatigue kills programs. Common mistakes: only running scans at release (too late), no triage SLAs, scanning without fixing, treating SAST as 'done' security, no business-logic testing. Senior move: integrate scans into developer flow (IDE + PR), establish SLAs by severity, automate dep updates, and pair tooling with **threat modeling + manual review** for the things automation can't catch.

sections.title: Security Testing Taxonomy
sections.content:
**Security testing** is umbrella for several distinct techniques, each finding different classes of issues at different cost/speed:

- **SAST (Static)** — analyzes source code or bytecode without running it. Catches code-level patterns: SQL injection, XSS, hardcoded secrets, weak crypto. Fast, runs in CI per commit. Tools: SonarQube, Semgrep, CodeQL, Snyk Code, SpotBugs + Find-Sec-Bugs, PMD security rules.
- **SCA (Software Composition Analysis)** — finds known vulnerabilities (CVEs) in third-party dependencies. Critical because most CVEs are in libs, not your code. Tools: Snyk, OWASP Dependency-Check, Dependabot, Renovate, JFrog Xray.
- **DAST (Dynamic)** — attacks the running application from outside; tests like a black-box attacker. Catches runtime issues: auth bypass, injection in form fields, security headers, TLS config. Tools: OWASP ZAP, Burp Suite, Acunetix, Netsparker.
- **IAST (Interactive)** — agent inside the running app instrumenting calls; combines SAST + DAST insight; very low false positives but more expensive. Tools: Contrast Security, Seeker, Synopsys.
- **Container scanning** — OS packages and base image CVEs. Tools: Trivy, Grype, Snyk Container, AWS ECR scanning.
- **IaC scanning** — misconfigurations in Terraform, K8s, CloudFormation. Tools: Checkov, tfsec, Terrascan, kube-score, kube-bench.
- **Secret scanning** — keys, tokens, passwords accidentally committed. Tools: gitleaks, trufflehog, GitHub secret scanning.
- **Penetration testing** — humans + creativity; chained exploits; business-logic bugs. Engaged quarterly or before major releases.
- **Bug bounty** — ongoing crowdsourced testing in production; HackerOne, Bugcrowd.
- **Fuzzing** — random or guided inputs to find crashes/edge cases; OSS-Fuzz, Jazzer for Java.

No single tool catches everything. **Coverage is the goal**: each technique catches what others miss.

sections.title: Security Testing Techniques Compared
sections.content:
| Technique | What it tests | When | Speed | Strengths | Weaknesses |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **SAST** | Source/bytecode patterns | PR / commit | Fast | Early, deep code coverage | False positives; misses runtime issues |
| **SCA** | Third-party deps for CVEs | PR / commit | Very fast | Catches most CVE risk | Reachability often unclear |
| **DAST** | Running app, black-box | Staging / nightly | Slow (minutes-hours) | Real runtime issues; auth flow | No code visibility; misses logic bugs |
| **IAST** | Running app, instrumented | During functional tests | Medium | Low FP; combines insight | Cost; needs agent in runtime |
| **Container scan** | Image OS packages, layers | Build / pre-deploy | Fast | Base image CVEs | App-layer code unaffected |
| **IaC scan** | Terraform/K8s configs | PR | Fast | Misconfig before deploy | Doesn't validate runtime |
| **Secret scan** | Repo history + commits | Pre-commit + PR | Fast | Prevents leaks | Doesn't catch already-leaked elsewhere |
| **Pen test** | Whole system | Quarterly / pre-major-release | Slow (days-weeks) | Chained, business-logic bugs | Expensive; point-in-time |
| **Bug bounty** | Production | Ongoing | Continuous | Real attackers, real motivation | Cost per finding; scope mgmt |
| **Fuzzing** | Inputs to functions/APIs | Nightly / continuous | Slow | Edge cases tools miss | Setup cost; coverage gaps |

sections.title: Practical Pipeline for a Spring Boot Service
sections.content:
**Stage 1: Developer flow (catch early)**
- IDE plugins: Sonarlint, Snyk, Semgrep show issues as you type
- Pre-commit hooks (`pre-commit` framework): gitleaks, ktlint/spotless, basic SAST
- `git secrets`-style hooks block commits with detected secrets

**Stage 2: PR pipeline (block bad code)**
```yaml
# .github/workflows/security.yml (excerpt)
jobs:
  sast:
    steps:
      - uses: returntocorp/semgrep-action@v1
        with:
          config: 'p/owasp-top-ten p/java p/spring'
      - uses: github/codeql-action/analyze@v3
        with:
          languages: java
  sca:
    steps:
      - uses: snyk/actions/maven@master
        env: { SNYK_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.SNYK_TOKEN }} }
        with:
          args: --severity-threshold=high
      - run: mvn org.owasp:dependency-check-maven:check
  secrets:
    steps:
      - uses: gitleaks/gitleaks-action@v2
```
Gate the PR: high/critical findings block merge; medium creates issue with SLA.

**Stage 3: Build (sign + scan artifacts)**
- Trivy / Grype scan container image
- Sign image with cosign (sigstore)
- Generate SBOM (`syft` or `cyclonedx-maven-plugin`)
- Reject deploys of unsigned/unscanned images via admission policy (Kyverno, OPA Gatekeeper)

**Stage 4: Staging (DAST + IAST)**
- ZAP baseline scan: passive analysis, security headers, basic injection
- ZAP full scan or Burp Suite Enterprise: active exploitation attempts
- IAST agent (Contrast, Seeker) during functional tests for low-FP findings
- IaC scan (Checkov, tfsec) on Terraform / Helm / K8s manifests

**Stage 5: Production (runtime + ongoing)**
- WAF (Cloudflare, AWS WAF): blocks common attacks before they reach app
- RASP (Runtime Application Self-Protection): runtime defense; monitor + block at app layer
- SIEM (Splunk, Elastic, Datadog Security): correlate logs, detect anomalies
- Periodic pen tests (quarterly minimum for production services)
- Bug bounty if mature (HackerOne, Bugcrowd) or private VDP first
- Continuous SCA: alerts when new CVEs disclosed for current dep versions

**Java-specific security tests**
```java
@SpringBootTest
@AutoConfigureMockMvc
class SecurityHeadersTest {
    @Autowired MockMvc mvc;

    @Test
    void enforcesSecurityHeaders() throws Exception {
        mvc.perform(get("/api/users"))
           .andExpect(header().exists("Strict-Transport-Security"))
           .andExpect(header().exists("Content-Security-Policy"))
           .andExpect(header().string("X-Frame-Options", "DENY"))
           .andExpect(header().string("X-Content-Type-Options", "nosniff"));
    }

    @Test
    @WithMockUser(roles = "USER")
    void cannotEscalateToAdmin() throws Exception {
        mvc.perform(get("/admin/users")).andExpect(status().isForbidden());
    }

    @Test
    void preventsSqlInjection() throws Exception {
        mvc.perform(get("/api/users/search?name=' OR '1'='1"))
           .andExpect(status().isBadRequest()); // or returns clean results
    }
}
```

These sit alongside functional tests and run on every PR.

sections.title: Triage, SLAs, Tuning, and Common Pitfalls
sections.content:
**Severity-driven SLAs**
- Critical (RCE, auth bypass, secret leak): fix in 24–48 hours; block deploys until fixed
- High (sensitive data exposure, privilege escalation): 7 days
- Medium (info disclosure, weak crypto in non-critical paths): 30 days
- Low (best practice violation, low-impact info disclosure): 90 days or accept

Automate ticket creation with severity + due date. Dashboards by team, by service. Failure to meet SLA escalates.

**Tuning is not optional**
- Initial deployment of any tool: hundreds of findings
- Triage in batches: which are real, which are FP, which are 'won't fix'
- Suppress FPs at the rule level, not by ignoring individual findings
- Tune custom rules to your codebase patterns (Semgrep / CodeQL custom queries)
- Re-tune quarterly; new patterns emerge

**Reachability matters for SCA**
- A CVE in a dep you don't actually call ≠ your CVE
- Snyk Reachability, Endor Labs, Backslash analyze whether vulnerable code is reachable
- Don't drop everything for unreachable CVEs; do prioritize reachable ones
- Still upgrade eventually; debt accumulates

**Pen test scoping**
- Define scope: white-box (with code/docs) vs gray-box vs black-box
- Time-box: typically 2–4 weeks for a complex service
- Authorized targets, hours, traffic limits
- Findings: documented, ranked, prioritized
- Re-test after fixes
- Use diverse vendors over time; different lenses

**Bug bounty maturity**
- VDP (Vulnerability Disclosure Policy) first: free, low-overhead, signals openness
- Private bounty: invited researchers; controlled scope
- Public bounty: open program; real volume; need triage capacity
- Don't start bug bounty without internal vuln management process; you'll drown

**Common pitfalls**

1. **Tool sprawl, no integration**: 5 tools, no triage owner, dashboards ignored
2. **Scan without fix**: findings pile up; nothing improves
3. **Only release-time scanning**: too late; expensive to fix; deploy gets blocked
4. **Severity inflation**: every finding marked critical = no real critical signal
5. **Treating SAST as security testing 'done'**: SAST misses runtime + business-logic issues
6. **Pen test once, never again**: code changes constantly; pen tests must too
7. **No internal training**: tools find issues developers don't know how to fix
8. **Ignoring container/IaC**: app code is clean but infra is misconfigured
9. **Bypassing scans for 'urgent' deploys**: creates a precedent
10. **No security champions**: AppSec team can't keep up alone; need embedded advocates
11. **Not testing third-party services / APIs you depend on**: their issues become yours
12. **Skipping authn/authz tests**: most common real-world bug class

**Threat modeling complements automated testing**
- Tools find known patterns; humans + threat modeling find what the system specifically allows wrong
- 30-min threat model per feature → derives custom test cases
- Combines well with abuse cases (negative testing)

**Build vs buy**
- Open source (Semgrep, ZAP, OWASP DC, gitleaks, Trivy) covers most needs
- Commercial (Snyk, Veracode, Checkmarx, Contrast) adds: managed rules, support, integration, reachability, IAST
- For most teams: open source baseline + 1–2 commercial for SCA / IAST

sections.title: Strategic View and Senior Engineer Moves
sections.content:
**The maturity ladder**
1. SCA in CI (Dependabot/Renovate + Snyk)
2. Secret scanning pre-commit + CI
3. SAST in CI (Semgrep / Sonar / Snyk Code)
4. Container scanning at build (Trivy)
5. IaC scanning (Checkov / tfsec)
6. DAST baseline scans on staging
7. Authz / security integration tests in app
8. Periodic pen tests
9. IAST during integration tests
10. Bug bounty (private → public)
11. Fuzzing for high-risk components
12. RASP / runtime monitoring + SIEM

Most teams should be 1–7; 8+ for high-risk / regulated.

**False positive management**
- Track FP rate per tool; tune until <20%
- Above that, devs ignore alerts; signal is lost
- A tool with high FP is worse than no tool: false confidence
- Custom rules > default rules; tune to your code

**Speed matters**
- SAST in PR: <5 min ideal
- SCA: <3 min
- Container scan: <2 min
- DAST baseline: <15 min
- DAST full: nightly
- Slower scans → dev frustration → workarounds

**Coverage matters**
- Don't just scan main branch; scan PR branches
- Don't just scan code; scan deps, containers, IaC, configs
- Don't just scan compiled artifact; instrument running app (IAST/RASP)

**Security as code review**
- Security checklist in PR template (auth changes, new deps, crypto, PII handling)
- Security champion on PR review for sensitive areas
- Document past incidents in a 'gotchas' file new hires read

**Compliance integration**
- PCI-DSS requires SAST + DAST + pen test
- HIPAA: similar
- SOC2: documented testing + remediation evidence
- ISO 27001: regular vuln assessment
- Map findings + fixes to compliance evidence; auditors love this

**Senior engineer moves**
- **Build a pipeline, not a checklist**: integrate scans into existing CI/CD
- **Tune aggressively**: every FP that lingers erodes trust
- **Set + enforce SLAs**: visible dashboards, escalation
- **Establish severity definitions**: shared language between security + eng
- **Pair tools with humans**: threat model, code review, pen test for what tools miss
- **Train developers**: secure coding workshops; OWASP Top 10 walkthroughs; internal CTF
- **Champion vulnerability triage**: treat security findings like bugs in the backlog
- **Measure**: MTTR by severity, finding rate, % deploys with security gates passing
- **Automate dep updates**: most CVEs fixed by upgrade; Renovate/Dependabot
- **Plan for incidents**: response runbooks; communication plan; legal contacts

**Strategic take**
- Security testing is a portfolio, not a single tool
- Layered defense: SAST + SCA + DAST + IAST + container/IaC + pen test + bug bounty
- Speed + low FP rate + clear SLAs = sustainable program
- Combine automated tooling with manual review + threat modeling
- Senior engineers integrate security into every stage — not as a gate at the end

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Security testing is layered**: SAST + SCA + DAST + IAST + container/IaC + secret scan + pen test + bug bounty
- Each catches **different classes** of issues at different cost/speed
- **Pipeline placement**: pre-commit → PR (SAST/SCA/secrets) → build (container/SBOM/sign) → staging (DAST/IAST/IaC) → prod (WAF/RASP/SIEM/pen test)
- **Severity-driven SLAs**: critical 24-48h, high 7d, medium 30d, low 90d
- **Tune aggressively** to minimize false positives; FP fatigue kills programs
- **Reachability** matters for SCA (Snyk Reachability, Endor Labs)
- **Pen testing + bug bounty** find what tools can't (logic, chained exploits)
- **Threat modeling complements** automated tests
- Java-specific: Semgrep + Snyk + Trivy + ZAP + Spring Security tests + Find-Sec-Bugs
- **Anti-patterns**: tool sprawl, scan-without-fix, severity inflation, only release-time, no triage owner
- **Maturity ladder**: SCA → secrets → SAST → container → IaC → DAST → IAST → pen → bounty
- Senior move: integrate into developer flow + clear SLAs + tune + train + automate

speakable_v2.hook: Security testing is a layered set of techniques, not one tool.

beats.text: Security testing is umbrella for several distinct techniques, each finding different classes of issues at different cost/speed: SAST (Static) — analyzes source code or bytecode without running it. Catches code-level patterns: SQL injection, XSS, hardcoded secrets, weak crypto. Fast, runs in CI per commit. Tools: SonarQube, Semgrep, CodeQL, Snyk Code, SpotBugs + Find-Sec-Bugs, PMD security rules. SCA (Software Composition Analysis) — finds known vulnerabilities (CVEs) in third-party dependencies. Critical because.

items: | Technique | What it tests | When | Speed | Strengths | Weaknesses | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | SAST | Source/bytecode patterns | PR / commit | Fast | Early, deep code coverage | False positives

misses runtime issues | | SCA | Third-party deps for CVEs | PR / commit | Very fast | Catches most CVE risk | Reachability often unclear | | DAST | Running app, black-box | Staging / nightly | Slow (minutes-hours) | Real runtime issues
misses logic bugs | | IAST | Running app, instrumented | During functional tests | Medium | Low FP

needs agent in runtime | | Container scan | Image OS packages, layers | Build / pre-deploy | Fast | Base image CVEs | App-layer code unaffected | | IaC scan | Terraform/K8s configs | PR | Fast | Misconfig before deploy | Doesn't validate runtime | | Secret scan | Repo history + commits | Pre-commit + PR | Fast | Prevents leaks | Doesn't catch already-leaked elsewhere | | Pen test | Whole system | Quarterly / pre-major-release | Slow (days-weeks) | Chained, business-logic bugs | Expensive
point-in-time | | Bug bounty | Production | Ongoing | Continuous | Real attackers, real motivation | Cost per finding
scope mgmt | | Fuzzing | Inputs to functions/APIs | Nightly / continuous | Slow | Edge cases tools miss | Setup cost

beats.text: The maturity ladder 1. SCA in CI (Dependabot/Renovate + Snyk) 2. Secret scanning pre-commit + CI 3. SAST in CI (Semgrep / Sonar / Snyk Code) 4. Container scanning at build (Trivy) 5. IaC scanning (Checkov / tfsec) 6. DAST baseline scans on staging 7. Authz / security integration tests in app 8. Periodic pen tests 9. IAST during integration tests 10. Bug bounty (private → public) 11. Fuzzing for high-risk components 12. RASP / runtime monitoring + SIEM Most teams should be 1–7; 8+ for high-risk / regulated. False.
